title: Hubble image of Messier 77
caption: The spiral galaxy Messier 77, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Messier 77 · constellation Cetus · about 45 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA & A. van der Hoeven

recognition.text: Ranked #64 on ESA/Hubble’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: Streaks of red and blue pick out pockets of star formation along the pinwheeling arms of this galaxy, while dark dust lanes stretch across its starry center. This is Messier 77, a spiral galaxy about 45 million light-years away in the constellation Cetus, photographed by Hubble.

M77 is a Seyfert galaxy, a class with an intensely active center wrapped in highly ionized gas. Ionized gas has had electrons stripped from its atoms, which happens when it is bathed in strong radiation.

In this picture, the arms, star-forming pockets and dust lanes are the familiar features of a spiral. The Seyfert label instead describes the intense activity at the galaxy's very center and the highly ionized gas around it. Hubble recorded the galaxy through visible, near-infrared and hydrogen-alpha filters.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.46 x 1.94 arcminutes) and distance (45 million light years), the frame spans roughly 32,000 × 25,000 light-years. Its light set out about 45 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's ACS and WFPC2 observed in visible, near-infrared and hydrogen-alpha light. Beyond the red and blue streaks marking star formation, the color mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared filter records light the eye cannot see, and the hydrogen-alpha filter isolates the glow of hydrogen gas.
